cmimc-2025-geometry-01.title: Fit the parallelogram along the diagonal
cmimc-2025-geometry-01.body:
A parallelogram net of a regular tetrahedron of side $x$ consists of four equilateral triangles: it has sides $x$ and $2x$ and angles $60^\circ,120^\circ$. It is biggest when its two far corners sit on opposite corners of the square, so that its long diagonal equals the square's diagonal $7\sqrt2$.

By the law of cosines the long diagonal of the parallelogram is $\sqrt{x^2+4x^2+2\cdot x\cdot2x\cdot\tfrac12}=x\sqrt7$. So $x\sqrt7=7\sqrt2$, giving $x^2=14$. (A numerical check over all rotations confirms this placement is optimal.)

The surface area of the tetrahedron is $4\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{4}x^2=14\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $14\sqrt3$**

cmimc-2025-geometry-02.title: Use the corner spheres
cmimc-2025-geometry-02.body:
The eight spheres sit in the corners, with centers at the vertices of a cube of side $2$ (centered at the center of the big cube); adjacent spheres are tangent since the centers are $2$ apart. The central sphere is centered at the center of the cube, whose distance to each of these centers is half the space diagonal $2\sqrt3$, namely $\sqrt3$. External tangency means $r+1=\sqrt3$, so $r=\sqrt3-1$.

**Answer: $\sqrt3-1$**

cmimc-2025-geometry-03.title: Coordinates
cmimc-2025-geometry-03.body:
Put $A=\left(-\frac12,0\right)$, $B=\left(\frac12,0\right)$. Then $C,D=\left(0,\pm\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$ and $CD=\sqrt3$. The circles about $C$ and $D$ of radius $\sqrt3$ meet on the $x$-axis at $E,F=\left(\mp\frac32,0\right)$, so $EF=3$. The circles about $E,F$ of radius $3$ meet at $G,H=\left(0,\pm\frac{3\sqrt3}2\right)$ (each step rotates by $90^\circ$ and scales by $\sqrt3$).

The pentagon $ACFHE$ (with $E$ on the left, $F$ on the right, $H$ at the bottom) splits along line $EF$ into triangle $EHF$ below it and triangle $ACF$ above it:
- $[EHF]=\frac12\cdot3\cdot\frac{3\sqrt3}2=\frac{9\sqrt3}4$,
- $[ACF]=\frac12\cdot AF\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}2=\frac12\cdot2\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}2=\frac{\sqrt3}2$.

Total: $\frac{9\sqrt3}4+\frac{2\sqrt3}4=\frac{11\sqrt3}4$.

**Answer: $\frac{11\sqrt3}{4}$**

cmimc-2025-geometry-04.title: Area of a triangle
cmimc-2025-geometry-04.body:
In trapezoid $AGHF$ the parallel sides cannot be $AF$ and $GH$ (that would put $H$ outside the hexagon), so $AG\parallel HF$. Then triangles $AGH$ and $AGF$ have the same area (same base $AG$, same height). Lines $AF$ and $CD$ are opposite sides of the hexagon, a distance $\sqrt3$ apart, so the altitude from $G$ (on $CD$) to $AF$ is $\sqrt3$. So $[AGF]=\frac12\cdot1\cdot\sqrt3=\frac{\sqrt3}2$.

By coordinates $A=(1,0)$, $G=\left(-\frac34,\frac{\sqrt3}4\right)$ so $AG=\sqrt{\frac{49}{16}+\frac3{16}}=\frac{\sqrt{13}}2$. The altitude is $h=\frac{2[AGH]}{AG}=\frac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt{13}/2}=\frac{2\sqrt3}{\sqrt{13}}=\frac{2\sqrt{39}}{13}$.

**Answer: $\frac{2\sqrt{39}}{13}$**

cmimc-2025-geometry-05.title: Locate the outer intersection points
cmimc-2025-geometry-05.body:
Let $AB=1$. Each ellipse is $\{P: PX+PY=2\}$ for its two foci. The ellipses $\mathcal E_{AB},\mathcal E_{AC}$ meet where $PA+PB=PA+PC=2$, so $PB=PC$: $P$ is on the axis of symmetry through $A$. The outer such point $G$ lies beyond $A$ (the other one is inside, where the triangle's edges would be crossed). Similarly $H$ is beyond $B$ on the axis through $B$ and $I$ beyond $C$. By symmetry $GHI$ is equilateral, and $GH\parallel AB$.

Since $G$ is on the ray from the center through $A$, $\angle GAB=150^\circ$. Let $GA=x$; then $GB=2-x$ and the law of cosines in $\triangle GAB$ gives $(2-x)^2=x^2+1+\sqrt3\,x$, so $x=\frac3{4+\sqrt3}$.

Projecting onto $AB$, $GH=1+2x\cos30^\circ=1+\sqrt3x=\frac{4+4\sqrt3}{4+\sqrt3}=\frac{4+12\sqrt3}{13}$. Since $AB=1$ the ratio is $\frac{12\sqrt3+4}{13}\approx1.906$ (numerical intersection of the ellipses agrees).

**Answer: $\frac{12\sqrt3+4}{13}$**

cmimc-2025-geometry-06.title: Coordinates along the three chords
cmimc-2025-geometry-06.body:
Take $X$ as origin and the chords along the axes: $A=(1,0,0)$, $B=(-b,0,0)$, $C=(0,\sqrt2,0)$, $D=(0,-d,0)$, $E=(0,0,2)$, $F=(0,0,-f)$ with $b,d,f>0$. The center is $O=\left(\frac{1-b}2,\frac{\sqrt2-d}2,\frac{2-f}2\right)$ (equidistant from the endpoints of each chord). All six points are on the sphere iff the power of $X$ is the same for the three chords: $1\cdot b=\sqrt2\,d=2f=k$. So $b=k$, $d=\frac k{\sqrt2}$, $f=\frac k2$.

Then $R^2=OA^2=\left(\frac{1+b}2\right)^2+\left(\frac{\sqrt2-d}2\right)^2+\left(\frac{2-f}2\right)^2=OX^2+k$ (since $\left(\frac{1+b}2\right)^2-\left(\frac{1-b}2\right)^2=b$), i.e. $R^2=\frac12+k$.

The condition $OX^2=\frac12$ reads $\frac14\left[(1-k)^2+\left(\sqrt2-\frac k{\sqrt2}\right)^2+\left(2-\frac k2\right)^2\right]=\frac12$, i.e. $\frac{7k^2}{4}-6k+7=2$, so $7k^2-24k+20=0$, $(k-2)(7k-10)=0$: $k=2$ or $k=\frac{10}7$.

Both give valid configurations, so $R^2=\frac52$ or $\frac{27}{14}$, with sum $\frac{35+27}{14}=\frac{31}7$.

**Answer: $\frac{31}7$**

cmimc-2025-geometry-07.title: Reflect A over BC
cmimc-2025-geometry-07.body:
Let $K$ be the reflection of $A$ over $BC$. From $B'X=B'A$ and $C'A=C'Y$ one gets (by equal arcs) $\angle B'AX=\angle ABC$ and $\angle C'AY=\angle ACB$; extending $YC$ and $XB$ they meet at $K$. Then $AK$ (which contains $F$, $P$) is the radical axis of $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$, hence $B,C,X,Y$ are concyclic.

With $A\in XY$, angle chasing gives $\angle KAX=\angle KBP$ and $\angle KAY=\angle KCP$, which sum to $180^\circ$, so $K,B,P,C$ are concyclic. By power of the point $F$: $FB\cdot FC=FK\cdot FP$.

Heron: area of $ABC$ is $\sqrt{10\cdot5\cdot2\cdot3}=10\sqrt3$, so $AF=\frac{2\cdot10\sqrt3}7=\frac{20\sqrt3}7=FK$. Also $BF=\frac{25-64+49}{14}=\frac57$ and $CF=7-\frac57=\frac{44}7$. Then $\frac57\cdot\frac{44}7=\frac{20\sqrt3}7\cdot FP$, so $FP=\frac{11\sqrt3}{21}$ and
$$PA=AF-FP=\frac{20\sqrt3}7-\frac{11\sqrt3}{21}=\frac{49\sqrt3}{21}=\frac{7\sqrt3}3.$$

**Answer: $\frac{7\sqrt3}3$**

cmimc-2025-geometry-07.title: Numerical check
cmimc-2025-geometry-07.body:
Placing $B=(0,0)$, $C=(7,0)$ and sliding $P$ along $AF$, computing $\omega_1,\omega_2,B',C',X,Y$ and testing collinearity of $X,Y,A$ numerically gives $PA\approx4.04=\frac{7\sqrt3}3$.

**Answer: $\frac{7\sqrt3}3$**

cmimc-2025-geometry-08.title: L lies on AB
cmimc-2025-geometry-08.body:
Let $J$ be the point on $AB$ with $BJ=13$, $AJ=7$, so $JB=CB$ and $JA=DA$. The circle through $C,D,J$ meets $AB$ again at $X$. Angle chasing ($\angle CJB=\angle JCB=\angle CDX$, and similarly at $A$) shows $DX$ and $CX$ bisect the exterior angles of $\triangle ECD$ at $D$ and $C$, so $X$ is the $E$-excenter: $L=X$ lies on $AB$.

Since $L$ is on the bisector of $\angle CED=\angle AEB$, it is the point of $AB$ with $\frac{AL}{LB}=\frac{EA}{EB}=\frac{\sin\angle EBA}{\sin\angle EAB}=\frac{\sin\angle CBA}{\sin\angle DAB}$. As $\angle ADB=\angle ACB=90^\circ$: $\cos\angle DAB=\frac7{20}$, $\sin\angle DAB=\frac{\sqrt{351}}{20}$, $\cos\angle CBA=\frac{13}{20}$, $\sin\angle CBA=\frac{\sqrt{231}}{20}$.

Thus $AL=\frac{20\sqrt{231}}{\sqrt{231}+\sqrt{351}}$ and
$$OL=10-AL=\frac{10(\sqrt{351}-\sqrt{231})}{\sqrt{351}+\sqrt{231}}=\frac{10(\sqrt{351}-\sqrt{231})^2}{120}=\frac{582-18\sqrt{1001}}{12}=\frac{97-3\sqrt{1001}}2\approx1.0421.$$

**Answer: $\frac{97-3\sqrt{1001}}2$**

cmimc-2025-geometry-08.title: Coordinate check
cmimc-2025-geometry-08.body:
With $O=(0,0)$, $A=(-10,0)$, $B=(10,0)$, computing $C,D,E$ and the excenter $L=\frac{-CD\cdot E+ED\cdot C+EC\cdot D}{-CD+ED+EC}$ gives $OL=1.0421239\ldots$, equal to $\frac{97-3\sqrt{1001}}{2}$.

**Answer: $\frac{97-3\sqrt{1001}}2$**

cmimc-2025-geometry-09.title: Affine squashing
cmimc-2025-geometry-09.body:
An ellipse is an affine image of a circle, so we look for the affine map that makes $ABCD$ cyclic while distorting the least; the ratio of the ellipse is then the stretching factor $k$ of that map (along its axis). Under an affine map parallel sides stay parallel, so the image is a cyclic trapezoid, hence isosceles: we need $A'D'=B'C'$.

Changing $AB$ and $CD$ by the same amount while sliding $BC$ does not matter, so reduce to a right triangle $XYZ$ with legs $XY=33$ ($=AD$) and $YZ=112$ ($=CD-AB$), with $XZ$ playing the role of $BC$: we need a squashing making $X'Y'=X'Z'$. With $M$ the midpoint of $YZ$ this means $X'M'\perp Y'Z'$.

Scale about $M$ by a factor $k$ perpendicular to a line $\ell$ making angles $\theta$ and $\gamma$ with $MY$ and $MX$. We need $\tan\theta'\tan\gamma'=-1$ where $\tan\theta'=k\tan\theta$ etc., i.e. $\tan\theta\tan\gamma=-\frac1{k^2}$. With $\gamma=\theta+\arctan\frac{33}{56}$ and $t=\tan\theta$, minimizing over $\theta$ (AM-GM, optimum at $x=1-\frac{33}{56}t=\frac{65}{56}$) gives $\max\left(-\tan\theta\tan\gamma\right)=\left(\frac{65-56}{33}\right)^2=\left(\frac3{11}\right)^2$. Hence $\frac1{k^2}=\frac9{121}$ and $k=\frac{11}3$.

**Answer: $\frac{11}3$**

cmimc-2025-geometry-09.title: Numerical check
cmimc-2025-geometry-09.body:
Put $D=(0,0)$, $C=(130,0)$, $A=(0,33)$, $B=(18,33)$. The conics through the four points form a one-parameter family $x^2+\frac{336}{99}xy+cy^2-130x-33cy=0$. For each $c$ (ellipse when $c>\left(\frac{168}{99}\right)^2$) the axis ratio is $\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}}$ of the quadratic form; minimizing over $c$ gives $3.66667=\frac{11}3$.

**Answer: $\frac{11}3$**

cmimc-2025-geometry-10.title: Show l is parallel to JQ
cmimc-2025-geometry-10.body:
$JQ$ is the Simson line of $P$. Let $PQ$ meet $\omega$ again at $L'$; angle chasing ($P,J,Q,C$ concyclic) shows $BL'\parallel JQ$. Trigonometry gives $BL'=8x+6y$ and $BP=8x-6y$. Computing $XQ$, $JQ=6y$, $BJ$ and using mass points on $\triangle BQC$ together with the power-of-a-point relations coming from the cyclic quadrilateral $BJUM$ leads to the stated polynomial relation for $\theta$; the dual Desargues involution theorem on the degenerate quadrilateral $ABIC$ then shows that $l=BI\parallel JQ$. Hence $L=L'$ and
$$BL=8x+6y=8(0.72951)+6(0.684)\approx9.94.$$

**Answer: about 9.94**

cmimc-2025-geometry-10.title: Numerical check
cmimc-2025-geometry-10.body:
Placing $B=(0,0)$, $C=(8,0)$, $A=(0,6)$ and solving $\cos\angle QJC=0.72951$ for $P$ on the lower arc, then taking $l\parallel JQ$ through $B$, one finds that $B,J,U,M$ are indeed concyclic (determinant $\approx0$) and $BL\approx9.9399$.

**Answer: 9.94**

cmimc-2025-geometry-11.title: Sum of arctangents
cmimc-2025-geometry-11.body:
The circle of radius $r_i=2^{-i}$ is tangent to both $PA_i$ and $PA_{i+1}$ at distance $2$ from $P$, so its center lies on the bisector of $\angle A_iPA_{i+1}$ and $\tan\frac{\angle A_iPA_{i+1}}2=\frac{r_i}2=2^{-i-1}$. Hence
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\angle A_0PA_n=\sum_{i\ge0}2\arctan\left(2^{-i-1}\right)=2\sum_{j\ge1}\arctan 2^{-j}\approx1.915777.$$
(The official answer is $1.91578$, found by graphing.)

**Answer: $1.915777$**
